title: Agentic AI Patterns: SAGA and Blackboard
oneLiner: AI agents don't just answer, they act. When several agents or services share a multi-step task, SAGA and blackboard patterns keep the work coordinated and recoverable.

what.html:
An AI agent is given a goal and works out the steps itself: it plans, uses tools such as search or email, remembers context and keeps going until it's done. When a task is split across many services or agents, the SAGA pattern runs it as a chain of steps with an "undo" for each, and the blackboard pattern lets specialists build a solution together on a shared board.

Everyday versionA chatbot is a travel guidebook; an agent is a travel agent who actually books things. A SAGA is like booking flight, hotel and car: if the car can't be booked, you cancel the hotel and flight. A blackboard is a team of detectives each pinning clues to one board.

why.html:
• Agents act in real systems (payments, email, code), so half-finished work can cause real damage.
  • Ordinary database rollbacks don't work across separate services; each has already saved its part.
  • Choosing central control or event-based coordination decides how easy the system is to debug and scale.

how.title: Chatbots answer, agents do
how.html: A chatbot replies to one message at a time and forgets. An agent pursues a goal over many steps, uses tools and keeps memory. Generative AI + reasoning + tools + feedback loops = agentic AI.

how.title: Inside an agent
how.html: An LLM does the thinking; memory keeps the conversation (short-term) and past facts (long-term); planning breaks the goal into steps; tools let it search, run code or call APIs. It loops: observe, think, act, reflect. Tools are called with small JSON messages such as {"tool_name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Bangalore"}}.

how.title: Four kinds of memory
how.html: Working memory is the current conversation (gone when the session ends). Episodic memory stores past interactions with this user. Semantic memory holds facts and rules. Procedural memory is know-how: instructions, tool definitions and workflows.

how.title: SAGA: steps with an undo button
how.html: Creating an order, taking payment, updating stock and shipping happen in different services, each saving its own change. If shipping fails, there's nothing to "roll back" automatically, so the SAGA runs compensating actions in reverse: restore stock, refund payment, cancel the order.

how.title: Conductor or dance?
how.html: Orchestration: a supervisor (a workflow engine, or a supervisor agent) tells each worker what to do and handles failures. Choreography: each worker listens for events and publishes its own; nobody is in charge. For agents, choreography looks like prompt chaining: each step's output triggers the next, and a flawed step is retried, reverted or refined.

how.title: The blackboard
how.html: For messy problems with no fixed recipe, put a shared board in the middle. Specialist agents read it and add their piece when they can; a controller decides who goes next and stops when the answer is complete. Agents never talk to each other directly.

demo.html: Run the research-paper workflow on the blackboard. With a well-formed paper the controller picks validation, then review, then summary. With a weak paper validation rejects it and nothing else runs, because no other agent's precondition is met.

example.html:
Travel-booking agent. Goal: "Book me a 3-day Goa trip under ₹40,000." A supervisor agent delegates to a flight agent, a hotel agent and a payment agent (orchestration). The flight is booked (T1), the hotel is booked (T2), payment fails (T3). The supervisor runs compensations in reverse: cancel the hotel (C2), cancel the flight (C1), and tells the user. Every step's state was saved, so a crash halfway can be resumed or compensated.

Supplementary Put irreversible steps (sending a confirmation email) last, and ask the user before any payment: compensation can't unsend an email.

misunderstandings: An agent is just a chatbot with a longer prompt.
Agents loop, use tools, keep memory and act on systems.
The model runs the tools itself.
It proposes a structured call; the host program executes it.
Compensation is the same as a rollback.
It's a new action that semantically undoes a committed step.
Choreography is always better because it's decoupled.
It's harder to trace; orchestration is clearer for complex flows.
Blackboard agents pass work to each other.
They only read and write the shared board; a controller schedules them.
takeaways: Agentic AI = generative AI + reasoning + tools + feedback loops.
Agents combine an LLM core, memory, planning, tools and an observe-think-act-reflect loop.
SAGA: local transactions plus compensating transactions run in reverse on failure.
Orchestration uses a central coordinator; choreography uses events without one.
Blackboard: specialists contribute partial solutions to a shared board under a controller.
thirty: Agentic AI systems pursue goals with limited supervision: an LLM reasons and plans, memory keeps working, episodic, semantic and procedural knowledge, tools are called with structured JSON, and an observe-think-act-reflect loop runs until the goal is met. When such work spans several services or agents, the SAGA pattern executes it as local transactions that each trigger the next and, if one fails, runs compensating transactions for the committed steps in reverse order. A SAGA can be orchestrated by a central coordinator, such as Step Functions or a supervisor agent, or choreographed through events, which for agents resembles prompt chaining. The blackboard pattern handles open-ended problems: specialist agents write partial results to a shared board and a controller decides who acts next.
